strengths: The method addresses a useful computer vision problem with a practical pipeline: compute representative teacher features, then synthesize images using feature matching and classwise BatchNorm regularization without bi-level optimization.
The reported high-resolution results are promising. At 50 images per class, Table 1 reports 59.4% on Tiny-ImageNet and 57.6% on ImageNet-1K, compared with CDA’s 48.7% and 53.5%, respectively.

Evaluation spans three datasets and multiple compression levels, with repeated measurements, component ablations, regularization sensitivity, and transfer to larger ResNet architectures. The visual examples also suggest improved within-class diversity.

The high-level pipeline is understandable, and foundational optimal-transport methods, SRe²L, POT, and source datasets are credited. The appendices appropriately acknowledge pretrained-classifier dependence, computational overhead, and propagation of dataset biases.
weaknesses: The experiments do not convincingly attribute the headline gains to Wasserstein matching. In Table 3, cross-entropy plus classwise BatchNorm without barycenter matching already achieves 64.0/41.3/37.4%, versus 64.8/41.8/38.2% for the complete method. More concerning, the ImageNet 10-IPC baseline described in the ablation achieves 36.1%, whereas Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe²L. This unexplained discrepancy changes the apparent improvement substantially. Matched training protocols and ablations at 50/100 IPC are needed.

The relationship to ordinary clustering is not addressed. With one empirical target distribution, squared-Euclidean cost, and freely optimized support weights, Eqs. (7)–(10) reduce to k-means quantization. Thus, the distinctive contribution beyond clustering teacher features and reconstructing prototypes remains unclear. A k-means prototype baseline using the same feature extractor and BatchNorm regularization is particularly important.

The optimized distribution is disconnected from the final training dataset. Algorithm 2 learns nonuniform weights, but Algorithm 1 retains only the support locations, and no corresponding weighted sampling or student loss is described. Consequently, uniformly training on the recovered images need not preserve the probability measure optimized by the Wasserstein objective.

The optimization justification contains substantive gaps. The constant-Hessian argument in Section 4.2.2 establishes convexity only for a fixed transport plan, not for the Wasserstein objective after optimizing that plan. Algorithm 2 changes the weights and then reuses the previous transport plan for the position update without clarifying marginal consistency. Furthermore, simplex projection permits zero weights, making the stated inverse Hessian undefined. These details require a corrected algorithm and justification.

The MMD comparison does not isolate the metric. Section 5.5 removes augmentation and FKD differences but does not establish identical feature extractors and BatchNorm regularization. At 1 IPC, the squared-Wasserstein barycenter is simply the class feature mean, which is also the target of linear-MMD mean matching under identical features. The large reported gap therefore cannot establish a geometric advantage by itself. The broader criticism of MMD also overlooks characteristic kernels, which can distinguish distributions.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete. Appendix E specifies image-recovery settings but leaves barycenter initialization, iteration count, and step size unspecified. Table 6 evaluates efficiency only on ImageNette at 1 IPC and does not clearly identify which preprocessing stages are included. This provides limited support for the claimed small overhead on ImageNet at larger IPC values.
